title: Resistance and resistivity — temperature dependence
notes: Resistance is R = ρ L / A. A longer wire has more resistance. A thicker wire has less. Resistivity ρ is the material property, independent of the particular length and area.
The unit of resistivity is the ohm metre. A good conductor has a small resistivity. Glass and rubber have very large resistivities and are used as insulators.

For a metal over a moderate range, ρ = ρ_0 (1 + α ΔT), where α is the temperature coefficient. α is positive for metals, so heating raises the resistivity. More violent lattice vibrations scatter the electrons more often.
The same linear form is used for resistance if the size does not change: R = R_0 (1 + α ΔT). A copper winding in a hot motor has a higher resistance than the cold value on the label.

A semiconductor has a negative temperature coefficient. Heating frees more carriers, and the resistivity falls. That is why a thermistor can be used as a thermometer and why a semiconductor is not described by the metal formula with a positive α.

Alloys such as manganin are made so that α is nearly zero. They are used for standard resistors. Superconductors drop to zero resistance below a critical temperature, which is outside this linear formula.

keyPoints: Metals increase in resistivity when heated.
summary: Resistance is resistivity times length over area. Metals have a positive temperature coefficient, so ρ and R rise when they are heated. Semiconductors usually do the opposite because more carriers are freed. The linear formula is only for a limited temperature range.
